new_findings_today.title: Destination slugs that collide with an Indian state/UT name bypass the soft-404 handling on garbage month sub-routes, returning HTTP 200 (with noindex) instead of HTTP 404
new_findings_today.detail: Section A's regression probe of hi/destination/puducherry/99 (a garbage month value on a real destination slug) returned HTTP 200 instead of the expected 404 -- the response body is homepage-shaped content (og:title/title = the site's generic homepage title) carrying a noindex meta tag, not a real destination page and not a proper 404. Follow-up direct curl probing beyond the 10-URL sample confirmed this is reproducible on every tested destination slug that shares its name with an Indian state or union territory: puducherry, goa, sikkim, delhi, and chandigarh all return 200 on a garbage /99 month sub-route (both /en and /hi), while non-colliding slugs sampled the same way (anamalai, amritsar) correctly return 404 on the identical pattern. Likely root cause (not verified in code this session): a routing/rewrite rule for the /state/[slug] or /family/[state] family of routes appears to intercept these specific destination-slug values before the normal destination-month soft-404 logic runs, falling through to a generic page instead of the expected not-found handling.
new_findings_today.evidence: Section A CSV: hi/destination/puducherry/99 -> HTTP 200, noindex_meta=True, 112476 bytes (vs 9-byte 404 bodies for all other Section-A probes). Direct curl re-confirmation (outside the harness sample): en+hi/destination/{puducherry,goa,sikkim,delhi,chandigarh}/99 all 200; en+hi/destination/{anamalai,amritsar}/99 (non-colliding controls) both 404.
new_findings_today.recommendation: Have an engineer trace the routing precedence for destination slugs that collide with state/UT names -- likely in the dynamic [locale]/destination/[slug]/[month] route or a middleware rewrite that treats these slugs specially. Because the page already carries a noindex meta tag, there is no immediate SEO/indexing risk, but the wrong HTTP status code means any status-code-based monitoring (Search Console coverage reports, uptime/error-rate dashboards) will not see these as the not-found pages they should be. Worth a quick full sweep against the ~28 India state/UT names to find the complete affected slug list before fixing.

business_about_this_report.note: How this report gets made, for context:
items: This check runs on a daily schedule without anyone needing to trigger it by hand. It visits the live site the same way a real visitor would — loading pages, following links, and reading what actually comes back — rather than just checking that the underlying code looks correct.

Every number in this report comes from something measured today: a page that was actually loaded, a database query that was actually run, or a screen that was actually looked at. Nothing here is estimated or copied forward from a previous day without being re-checked.

Three versions of this report are produced from the same underlying checks: this plain-language version for a business owner, a more detailed version for whoever is doing QA review, and a fully technical version for whoever is fixing things day-to-day.

When something can't be checked for a good reason (for example, a check that would require submitting a real form, or a deeper review that's simply not due yet), that's stated plainly rather than skipped silently or guessed at.

This report and the two more technical companion reports are all regenerated from a single underlying set of today's results — none of the three re-runs any checks or re-measures anything independently.
If a number in this report looks surprising, the more detailed companion reports break every section down further, section by section, with the specific evidence behind each pass or fail.
